vignette:
Mr. A. is a seventy-five-year-old man who has been coming to see me for six weeks. He was referred by his primary care physician, who noted he had become increasingly withdrawn and had stopped attending the local temple, a place he had visited daily for the past twelve years. His wife, who accompanies him to our sessions and waits in the lobby, reports that he no longer sleeps in their bed, preferring the hard floor of his pottery studio.

He tells me his story slowly, in a voice that is soft and careful, as if he is still deciding whether the words are safe to speak aloud. He was born in a small village in what is now Bangladesh. He was a potter, as his father was, and his grandfather. He learned the wheel when he was seven years old. In 1971, when he was twenty-four, war came to his country. He does not say the name of the war. He does not need to.

One morning, soldiers arrived in his village. He was at his wheel, his hands covered in wet clay. He heard the shouting first, then the shots. He ran to the back of his house and hid in the kiln, the one he used for firing his pots. It was still warm from the previous night's work. He stayed there, curled into a ball, for what he thinks was two days. He could hear everything. The screams. The boots on the hard earth. The crackling of flames as his neighbors' homes burned. He tells me this part of the story while staring at his own hands, which are resting on his knees. They are thick and scarred, the hands of a man who has spent a lifetime shaping clay. They tremble slightly.

He eventually escaped. He walked for weeks. He crossed a river at night, holding onto a piece of driftwood. He ended up in a refugee camp in India. He spent three years there. He does not speak of those years. When I ask, he simply shakes his head. "Nothing," he says. "There was nothing."

He was resettled in the United States in 1974. He found work in a ceramics factory. He met his wife, a kind woman from a neighboring village, at a community gathering. They married, had two children, built a life. He never spoke of the war. He never spoke of the kiln. He built a studio in his garage and began making pots again. For decades, he was fine. He was busy.

But now, he is not fine. He tells me that six months ago, his grandson, a boy of sixteen, came to visit. The boy was taking a pottery class in school and wanted his grandfather to show him how to center the clay on the wheel. Mr. A. agreed. He sat down at his wheel. The boy stood beside him. Mr. A. put water on the clay. He pressed his palm into the spinning mass. And then, he says, the smell came back. The smell of wet earth and smoke. The smell of the kiln. The smell of that morning.

He had to stop. He had to leave the room. He went into the bathroom and stood over the sink, his heart pounding, his skin slick with sweat. He felt like he was back in that kiln, curled up, listening. He could hear the screams. He could smell the smoke. He could feel the heat of the fire on his face.

Since that day, he has not touched his wheel. He cannot enter his studio without feeling a wave of nausea. He has nightmares, almost every night. In the dreams, he is back in the kiln, but the kiln is also the studio, and his grandson is outside, calling for him, and he cannot move. He wakes up gasping, convinced he can smell smoke. He has started checking the stove in his kitchen three or four times before he can go to bed. He avoids the news. He avoids any mention of war or conflict. He has stopped going to the temple because the incense reminds him of the smoke.

He tells me he feels like a coward. He says he survived, he came here, he made a life. Why is he falling apart now? He looks at me with wet eyes. "I am a potter," he says. "I make things. I hold things. Now I cannot hold anything."
